module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1014

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1014](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1014)
- [Er71] Erdős, P., Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis. Combinatorial
  Mathematics and its Applications (Proc. Conf., Oxford, 1969) (1971), 97-109.
- [OpenAI26] *On the ratio of $R(k,\ell)$ and $R(k,\ell+1)$*, proof due to an internal model at
  OpenAI (2026).
  https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/6dc7175d-d9e7-4b8d-96b8-48fe5798cd5b/Ramsey.pdf
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

open scoped Topology

namespace Erdos1014

local notation "R(" k ", " l ")" => SimpleGraph.classicalRamsey k l

/--
Let $R(k,l)$ be the Ramsey number, so the minimal $n$ such that every graph on at least $n$
vertices contains either a $K_k$ or an independent set on $l$ vertices.

Prove, for fixed $k\geq 3$, that
$$\lim_{l\to \infty}\frac{R(k,l+1)}{R(k,l)}=1.$$

This has been
[solved](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/6dc7175d-d9e7-4b8d-96b8-48fe5798cd5b/Ramsey.pdf)
by an internal model at OpenAI.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1014.lean"]
theorem erdos_1014 : ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k →
    Tendsto (fun l : ℕ ↦ (R(k, l + 1) : ℝ) / (R(k, l) : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 1) := by
  sorry

/--
That proof in fact shows that
$$R(k,l+1)\leq (1+O(l^{-c/k^2}))R(k,l)$$
for some constant $c>0$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_1014.variants.upper_bound :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k → ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ᶠ l : ℕ in atTop,
      (R(k, l + 1) : ℝ) ≤ (1 + C * (l : ℝ) ^ (-c / (k : ℝ) ^ 2)) * (R(k, l) : ℝ) := by
  sorry

end Erdos1014

reformulations.difference: The source writes R(k,l+1) ≤ (1+O(l^{-c/k^2}))R(k,l) "for some constant c>0". The Lean makes c > 0 uniform in k. It then gives the big-O a constant C chosen after k (∃ C : ℝ, possibly negative) and an 'eventually in l' threshold that also depends on k. A reader might ask whether C should be uniform in k, or whether c should be allowed to depend on k (the paper's Remark 1 uses c_k).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For fixed k, 'f(l) = O(g(l)) as l→∞' is exactly '∃ C, eventually |f| ≤ C·g', and R(k,l) ≥ 0, so the Lean is the literal reading. Where C is placed makes no difference. Given C for some k, halve c: since l^{c/(2k^2)} → ∞, eventually C·l^{-c/k^2} ≤ l^{-(c/2)/k^2}. So the statement is equivalent to the version with C = 1, i.e. to a C that is uniform in k. I proved this ↔ in Lean for an arbitrary f : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ in place of R. Taking c uniform matches the source's c/k^2 wording and is true. From (3) in the OpenAI proof, the right-hand side is ≪_k ℓ^{-1/2}(log ℓ)^{k/2}, and taking k^2-th roots gives any c < 1/2. I also checked in Lean that l^{-c/k^2} → 0, so the variant really controls the ratio and is not vacuous.

reformulations.difference: R(k,l) is `SimpleGraph.classicalRamsey k l = sInf {n | ∀ C : SimpleGraph (Fin n), K_k ⊑ C ∨ K_l ⊑ Cᶜ}`. It is phrased with copies of complete graphs, on exactly n vertices. The source's R(k,l) is the minimal n such that every graph on at least n vertices contains a K_k or an independent set on l vertices.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Proved in Lean: classicalRamsey k l = sInf {n | ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), ¬(G.CliqueFree k ∧ Gᶜ.CliqueFree l)}, via `not_cliqueFree_iff_top_isContained`. Also proved: the defining set is upward closed (comap along Fin.castLEEmb), so classicalRamsey k l = sInf {n | ∀ m ≥ n, every graph on Fin m has K_k or an independent l-set}. By Ramsey's theorem the set is nonempty, so sInf is the true minimum. Sanity checks also proved: R(k,0) = 0 and R(k,1) = 1 for k ≥ 1. The only junk value on the path is l = 0, where the ratio is R(k,1)/0 = 0; that cannot affect the limit.
